title: Sunita Williams Leads New York Veterans Day Parade as Grand Marshal
excerpt: The retired NASA astronaut and Navy captain, who spent 608 days in space across three missions, headed the 107th annual parade up Fifth Avenue on November 11.
body:
• Retired NASA astronaut Sunita Williams served as Grand Marshal of the 107th New York City Veterans Day Parade on Wednesday, November 11, leading 20,000 participants up Fifth Avenue.
  • Williams, a retired US Navy captain of Indian and Slovenian descent, retired from NASA on December 27, 2025, after 27 years, 608 days in space and nine spacewalks — the most spacewalk time by any woman.
  • Her final mission, the first crewed flight of Boeing's Starliner in June 2024, stretched from a planned short test flight to 286 days aboard the International Space Station before she returned on a SpaceX Dragon in March 2025.
  • For diaspora readers: Williams, whose father Deepak Pandya was an Indian-born neuroanatomist, carried a copy of the Bhagavad Gita to the space station in 2006 and the Upanishads in 2012.

Sunita Williams led the 107th annual New York City Veterans Day Parade on Wednesday as its Grand Marshal, marching up Manhattan's Fifth Avenue at the head of 20,000 participants, according to wire reports of the event. The parade, produced by the United War Veterans Council and first held in 1919, stepped off at 12:30 p.m. at Fifth Avenue and 26th Street, following a wreath-laying ceremony in Madison Square Park. Thousands of veterans, armed-services contingents, law-enforcement units, community groups, schools and bands took part, with the US Navy as this year's featured service.

Williams, a retired Navy captain, was announced as Grand Marshal on the US Navy's birthday, in a year when the parade also marked the 250th birthday of the United States. The council's president and executive director, Mark Otto, said her "dedication and service embody the values we honor each Veterans Day." On the eve of the parade, Williams took part in commemorations of the 251st anniversary of the Marine Corps' founding aboard the USS San Antonio, according to IANS.

"It is an incredible honor to serve as Grand Marshal of the NYC Veterans Day Parade and to march alongside my fellow veterans. My time in the Navy shaped who I am and prepared me for every challenge that followed."

— Sunita Williams, Grand Marshal

A career that ended less than a year ago

The honour comes in Williams's first year out of uniform at NASA. She retired from the agency on December 27, 2025, after 27 years, NASA announced. Selected as an astronaut in 1998 after a Navy career that began with her commissioning in 1987 — she became a naval aviator in 1989 and later a test pilot — she flew three missions to the International Space Station, on Expeditions 14/15, 32/33 and 71/72. Her 608 cumulative days in space rank second on NASA's all-time list, and her nine spacewalks, totalling 62 hours and 6 minutes, are the most by a woman and fourth overall. She was also the first person to run a marathon in space.

Her last flight made her a household name well beyond the space community. She launched in June 2024 aboard Boeing's Starliner on its first crewed mission, a test flight expected to last days. After NASA decided to return Starliner uncrewed, Williams and crewmate Butch Wilmore stayed aboard the station for 286 days — tied as the sixth-longest single spaceflight by an American — with Williams commanding Expedition 72 before the pair returned to Earth in March 2025 aboard a SpaceX Crew-9 Dragon.

The Indian connection

Born in Euclid, Ohio, and raised in Needham, Massachusetts, Williams is the daughter of Deepak Pandya, a neuroanatomist born in India, and Ursuline Pandya, who is from Slovenia. She has spoken often about that heritage in orbit: she carried a copy of the Bhagavad Gita to the station in 2006 and the Upanishads in 2012. Her honours include the Padma Bhushan, the Defense Superior Service Medal and the Legion of Merit. Full parade details are on the United War Veterans Council's Grand Marshal page.

"Anyone who knows me knows that space is my absolute favorite place to be," Williams said when her retirement was announced. "I had an amazing 27-year career at NASA." On Wednesday, that career's second act — as one of the most visible Indian American veterans in public life — was on display in front of a Fifth Avenue crowd.
